# The Explosion You Can't Outrun: Counting the Hidden Symmetries of a Staircase

## A puzzle about shelves

Imagine a tall, narrow museum of crystals. Each crystal sits on a shelf, and the
shelves are stacked by "size." A crystal on a higher shelf is *bigger* than one
on a lower shelf only when one literally contains the other; crystals on the same
shelf are siblings that nobody ranks against each other. Mathematicians call such
a stack of comparisons a **partially ordered set**, or *poset*: some pairs are
comparable, many are not.

Now a curator walks in with a tidy-up rule. She wants to thread a single ribbon
through crystals so that each ribbon climbs strictly upward, one shelf at a time,
with no gaps — and she wants the whole ribbon to be **balanced**: it should start
as far below the middle shelf as it ends above it. A ribbon like this is called a
**symmetric chain**. Her goal is to cover *every* crystal with such ribbons, each
crystal on exactly one ribbon. A complete tidy-up of this kind is a **symmetric
chain decomposition** — an SCD for short.

Here is the question this article is about, and it sounds innocent:

> *In how many genuinely different ways can the museum be tidied up?*

Not "can it be done" — that is a famous and beautiful problem in its own right —
but *how many* distinct ways exist. Call that number $\#\mathrm{SCD}(P)$ for a
poset $P$. The astonishing answer, for the right family of posets, is that the
count doesn't just grow as the museum grows. It **detonates** — faster than any
fixed rate of compound interest you could ever name.

## Two ways things can grow

Before we open the museum, we need to be precise about the word "fast."

A bank that doubles your money every year grows *exponentially*: after $n$ years
you have $2^n$ dollars. A more aggressive bank tripling your money gives $3^n$.
You can pick any base $c$ you like — $10$, a million, a googol — and get $c^n$.
That is the whole family of **exponential** growth rates.

There is a kind of growth that beats *every* member of that family at once. We
say a sequence $f(n)$ is **super-exponential** if, no matter which base $c$ you
choose, eventually $f$ overtakes $c^n$ and stays ahead forever:

$$\text{for every } c, \text{ there is an } N \text{ so that } c^n < f(n) \text{ for all } n \ge N.$$

This is a strong demand. A super-exponential sequence cannot be matched by any
compound-interest scheme, however greedy. It is the mathematical signature of a
true combinatorial explosion.

The cleanest example is the **factorial**, $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots n$, the
number of ways to arrange $n$ books on a shelf. It starts out modest — $5! = 120$
— but it has a secret weapon: each new factor it multiplies by keeps *growing*.
An exponential $c^n$ multiplies by the same tired $c$ every step; the factorial
multiplies by $n$, then $n+1$, then $n+2$. Sooner or later $n$ exceeds $c$, and
from that moment the factorial pulls away and never looks back. Concretely, for
each base $c$ the ratio $c^n / n!$ slides to zero, so eventually $c^n < n!$. The
factorial is super-exponential, full stop.

And it carries a friend with it. The number of ways to **shuffle** a deck of $n$
distinct cards — to permute them — is exactly $n!$. So the count of shuffles is
super-exponential too. Hold on to that fact; the whole story turns on it.

## A transfer principle: ride the factorial's coattails

Super-exponential growth is contagious in a useful direction. Suppose you have
some mysterious counting sequence $g(n)$, and you cannot compute it exactly — but
you *can* prove that it is at least as big as the factorial from some point on,
$n! \le g(n)$. Then $g$ inherits the explosion automatically: it, too, is
super-exponential.

The reason is almost too simple. To beat $c^n$, the factorial eventually does so
on its own; and $g$ sits above the factorial; so $g$ beats $c^n$ as well. A
*lower bound* by a factorial is therefore a passport to super-exponential growth.
This little **transfer principle** is the lever we will use to pry open the
museum. We never need the exact count of tidy-ups — only a factorial-sized floor
underneath it.

## The simplest museum that explodes

Strip the museum down to two shelves. On the bottom shelf, $n$ crystals; on the
top shelf, $n$ crystals; and every bottom crystal is smaller than every top
crystal. Nothing on the same shelf is comparable. This barest of two-level
posets — its points are pairs $(\text{shelf}, \text{index})$, formally
$\{\text{bottom}, \text{top}\} \times \{1, \dots, n\}$ — is the **two-level
slab**.

What does a symmetric chain look like here? With only two shelves, a balanced
upward ribbon is just a single rung: pick one bottom crystal and one top crystal,
and join them. A complete tidy-up must cover all $2n$ crystals with such rungs,
each crystal used once. That means: pair up every bottom crystal with a distinct
top crystal. A perfect matching between bottoms and tops.

But a perfect matching between two labeled sets of size $n$ is *exactly a
permutation* — a way of deciding which top partner each bottom gets. And we
counted those already: there are $n!$ of them. So the simplest exploding museum
has its tidy-ups in one-to-one correspondence with shuffles of $n$ cards.

This is the heart of the formal result. Writing $\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$ for the
number of tidy-ups of the two-level slab, one builds an explicit, injective map

$$\text{shuffles of } n \text{ cards} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{tidy-ups of the slab},$$

sending each permutation to the matching it describes. Injectivity gives the key
inequality, proved rigorously:

$$n! \;\le\; \mathrm{numSCD}(n).$$

Feed that into the transfer principle, and the conclusion lands:

> **The number of symmetric chain decompositions of the two-level slab is
> super-exponential.**

The count outruns $2^n$, $1000^n$, and every $c^n$ you could ever write down. A
two-shelf museum with $n$ crystals per shelf has, hidden inside it, more distinct
tidy-up patterns than any exponential can keep pace with.

(Each tidy-up *really is* a distinct permutation, so one expects equality,
$\mathrm{numSCD}(n) = n!$, exactly. That sharper statement is left as a
conjecture; the inequality $n! \le \mathrm{numSCD}(n)$ is what is proved, and the
inequality is all the explosion needs.)

## Why it explodes: the arithmetic of independent choices

Stand back and ask *why* the factorial showed up. When you build a matching on
the slab, you choose a top partner for bottom crystal $1$ (n options), then for
bottom crystal $2$ (one fewer option), and so on. The choices are **independent
and numerous**, and crucially their *number grows with the size of the museum*.
With $n$ crystals you make roughly $n$ free decisions, and $n$ free decisions of
shrinking multiplicity multiply into $n!$.

That phrase — *the number of independent choices grows with $n$* — is the engine.
It is what separates explosion from mere fast growth. And the cleanest way to
appreciate it is to look at a structure that grows fast but, decisively, does
**not** explode.

## A foil: the crown that grows but never explodes

Consider a different exhibit, the **blown-up crown**. Fix a small width $w$ (think
$w = 2$ or $3$). The crown is a ring of $w$ "columns," each column a little
two-vertex gadget — a lower vertex $a$ and an upper vertex $b$ — wired so that the
lower vertex of one column relates to the upper vertex of the next, going around
the ring. Then *fatten* every vertex into a chain of $m$ identical clones stacked
on top of each other. The resulting poset, written $\mathrm{Crown}(w, m)$, has
exactly $2wm$ points, and — this is the subtle part — its **width stays exactly
$w$** no matter how large $m$ grows. Fattening into stacked chains adds bulk
without widening the poset.

Crowns are famous for a different combinatorial object: **strict alternating
cycles**, the zig-zag patterns of incomparability that drive the theory of poset
dimension. One can count, with a rigorous floor, how many such cycles the
blown-up crown carries. The answer is at least

$$m^{2w}.$$

Now watch the two knobs. As you turn up $m$ (more clones per vertex), this count
sails off to infinity — the crown genuinely grows without bound. But $2w$ is a
*fixed* exponent, frozen by the width. So $m^{2w}$ is a **polynomial** in $m$: a
cubic, a sixth power, whatever — but a fixed power. And a fixed power, however
large, is *never* super-exponential. You can always find a base $c$ whose $c^m$
eventually swamps any fixed $m^{2w}$. The crown grows, diverges, impresses — and
still loses the race to every exponential.

Here is the punchline, the synthesis the whole project is built to deliver, all
three clauses proved together:

> The two-level slab's tidy-up count is super-exponential; the crown's certified
> floor $m^{2w}$ is **not** super-exponential; and yet the crown's cycle count
> still diverges to infinity.

Two honest lower bounds on two poset-combinatorial counts. One explodes; one
merely grows. What is the difference between them?

## The dividing line

It is precisely the arithmetic of choices.

- In the **crown**, the number of independent choices is *bounded*: there are
  $2w$ columns to decide, fixed once and for all, each with $m$ options. That
  gives $m^{2w}$ — a fixed power, *bounded arity*, polynomial. It diverges in $m$
  but never beats an exponential.

- In the **slab**, the number of independent choices *grows with $n$*: you make
  about $n$ matching decisions, and the number of decisions climbs as the museum
  climbs. That gives $n!$ — *growing arity*, super-exponential.

Bounded arity makes polynomials. Growing arity makes factorials. That single
distinction — **does the number of free choices stay fixed, or does it grow?** —
is the structural insight, and it is now a theorem, not a slogan.

## Back to the staircase

Why does any of this matter beyond two-shelf toy museums? Because the two-level
slab is a microcosm of the *middle* of a far richer object. Take the lattice
$M(n)$ of all ways to write a number as a sum of **distinct** parts, each part at
most $n$ — equivalently, all subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, ranked by their
total. Its shelves swell toward the center: the middle ranks are enormous and
densely interconnected, and they look, locally, exactly like a fat two-level
slab. The same growing-arity mechanism should fire there.

That is the conjecture this work is aimed at, and that it makes precise and
partially formal: **the number of symmetric chain decompositions of $M(n)$ grows
super-exponentially in $n$** — and likewise for the classical minuscule lattices
$L(m, n)$ of partitions in an $m \times n$ box, for any fixed $m > 1$. These
lattices are known to *admit* a symmetric chain decomposition; the new claim is
about the sheer *abundance* of them. The middle slab supplies a growing number of
independent matching choices, and growing arity, as we now know, means explosion.

The contribution here is to forge the engine and bolt it down: a rigorous
definition of super-exponential growth; a proof that the factorial — and hence
the count of shuffles — clears that bar; a transfer principle that upgrades any
factorial-sized floor into super-exponential growth; a concrete two-level slab
whose tidy-ups number at least $n!$; and a sharp counterexample, the polynomial
crown floor, that proves the dividing line is real and not a mirage. The road
from here to $M(n)$ and $L(m, n)$ is to show their central shelves carry that same
growing supply of independent choices — a finite, rank-by-rank counting problem,
guided now by a theorem that tells us *exactly what to look for*.

## The moral

Counting is not one thing. Some collections grow quickly and are still, in the
end, tameable by a fixed exponential — the crown, forever a polynomial in
disguise. Others carry inside them a *growing* number of free, independent
decisions, and those collections explode past every exponential at once, the way
the humble factorial does. The number of ways to tidy a staircase of crystals is
of the second, wilder kind. Learning to read which kind you are facing — by
asking whether your choices are bounded or growing — is one of the quiet, powerful
lessons of combinatorics. The museum was never just a museum. It was a question
about how fast freedom multiplies.

# Super-Exponential Growth of Symmetric Chain Decomposition Counts: A Bounded-vs-Growing-Arity Dichotomy

**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-06-28
**Domain:** Novelty / Order theory & enumerative combinatorics

---

## Abstract

We study the *number* of symmetric chain decompositions (SCDs) of graded posets,
a finer invariant than the classical existence question. We isolate a clean
growth predicate, **super-exponentiality** — a sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{N}$ is super-exponential if it eventually dominates every fixed
exponential $c^n$ — and prove that it is generated by *growing arity of
independent combinatorial choices*. Concretely, we prove: (1) the factorial is
super-exponential, and hence so is the count of permutations of an $n$-element
set; (2) super-exponentiality transfers upward along eventual pointwise
inequalities, so any factorial-sized lower bound on a count forces
super-exponential growth; (3) a fixed polynomial $m \mapsto m^{k}$ is *not*
super-exponential. We then exhibit a concrete instance: the two-level "slab"
poset $\mathrm{CB}(n)$ on $\{\bot,\top\}\times\{1,\dots,n\}$ has at least $n!$
symmetric chain decompositions, via an explicit injection from the symmetric
group, whence its SCD-count $\mathrm{numSCD}$ is super-exponential. Finally we
contrast this with a catalog construction, the blown-up crown
$\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)$ of fixed width $w$: its certified floor of $m^{2w}$ strict
alternating cycles *diverges* yet is provably *not* super-exponential. The
synthesis theorem packages all three phenomena and pinpoints the dividing line:
super-exponential growth arises precisely when the number of independent choices
grows with the parameter (slab: $n$ matchings $\Rightarrow n!$), and fails when
that number is bounded (crown: $2w$ choices $\Rightarrow m^{2w}$). This furnishes
the structural engine behind the conjecture that $\#\mathrm{SCD}(M(n))$ — and,
for fixed $m>1$, $\#\mathrm{SCD}(L(m,n))$ — is super-exponential in $n$. All
results are machine-checked.

---

## 1. Introduction

A finite **graded poset** $P$ is a partially ordered set equipped with a rank
function $\mathrm{rk}:P\to\mathbb{N}$ such that covering relations increase rank
by one; let $N=\max_{x}\mathrm{rk}(x)$ be its top rank. A chain
$x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_k$ is **symmetric** if its ranks are consecutive,
$\mathrm{rk}(x_{i+1})=\mathrm{rk}(x_i)+1$, and balanced about the middle,
$\mathrm{rk}(x_0)+\mathrm{rk}(x_k)=N$. A **symmetric chain decomposition (SCD)**
of $P$ is a partition of $P$ into symmetric chains.

Symmetric chain decompositions are a cornerstone of Sperner theory: a poset
admitting an SCD is automatically Sperner, rank-symmetric, rank-unimodal, and has
the strong Sperner property. The *existence* of SCDs has been studied intensively
— famously for the Boolean lattice (de Bruijn–Tengbergen–Kruyswijk), for products
of chains, and for the normalized matching / LYM family.

This paper concerns a different and finer invariant: the **number**
$\#\mathrm{SCD}(P)$ of distinct symmetric chain decompositions. The motivating
conjecture, in the order-theoretic literature on minuscule lattices, asserts that
for fixed $m>1$ the count $\#\mathrm{SCD}(L(m,n))$ — where $L(m,n)$ is the lattice
of partitions fitting in an $m\times n$ box — grows *super-exponentially* in $n$.
An analogous conjecture is natural for $M(n)$, the lattice of partitions into
distinct parts at most $n$ (equivalently, subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ranked by
their sum).

### 1.1 Contributions

We do not resolve the $L(m,n)$ / $M(n)$ conjecture. Instead we build and verify
the *engine* such a proof must run on, and we identify the precise structural
mechanism responsible:

1. A rigorous, base-uniform definition of super-exponential growth
   (Definition 2), and the proof that the factorial — and the permutation count —
   clears it (Theorem 1, Corollary 1).
2. A **transfer principle** (Lemma 1): super-exponentiality propagates upward
   along eventual pointwise inequalities, converting any factorial lower bound on
   a count into super-exponential growth of that count.
3. A **non-vacuity / contrast** theorem (Theorem 2): fixed polynomials
   $m\mapsto m^k$ are not super-exponential — the predicate is a genuine dividing
   line.
4. A concrete realization (Theorems 3–4): the two-level slab $\mathrm{CB}(n)$ has
   $\mathrm{numSCD}(n)\ge n!$ via an explicit injection $\mathrm{permChains}$ from
   $\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)$, hence $\mathrm{numSCD}$ is super-exponential.
5. A **bridge to the catalog** (Theorems 5–7): the blown-up crown
   $\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)$ carries at least $m^{2w}$ strict alternating cycles
   (Theorem 5); this floor diverges (Theorem 6, divergence clause) yet is *not*
   super-exponential (Theorem 6, contrast clause); the synthesis (Theorem 7)
   packages the slab and crown side by side and exposes the dividing line.

The throughline is a **dichotomy**: *bounded arity of independent choices yields
polynomial floors; growing arity yields factorial floors and hence
super-exponential growth.*

---

## 2. The growth predicate

**Definition 1 (exponential domination).** A sequence $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$
*dominates the base-$c$ exponential eventually* if there is $N$ with $c^n<f(n)$
for all $n\ge N$.

**Definition 2 (super-exponential, `SuperExp`).** $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is
**super-exponential** if it dominates *every* fixed exponential eventually:
$$\mathrm{SuperExp}(f) \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; \forall c\in\mathbb{N},\ \exists N,\ \forall n\ge N,\ c^n < f(n).$$

The order of quantifiers matters: the threshold $N$ may depend on $c$, but a
*single* $f$ must beat *all* bases. This is the formal rendering of "grows faster
than any fixed exponential."

**Theorem 1 (`factorial_superexp`).** $\mathrm{SuperExp}(n\mapsto n!)$.

*Proof sketch.* Fix a base $c$. Cast to the reals and use the classical limit
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{c^n}{n!}=0$$
(in Lean, `FloorSemiring.tendsto_pow_div_factorial_atTop`). Unfolding the metric
definition of the limit at tolerance $\varepsilon=1$ yields an $N$ such that for
all $n\ge N$, $\bigl|c^n/n!\bigr|<1$, i.e. $c^n/n!<1$. Since $n!>0$, multiply
through to get $c^n<n!$ over $\mathbb{R}$, and descend to $\mathbb{N}$ by an
order-preserving cast. Hence $\forall n\ge N,\ c^n<n!$. $\square$

A purely combinatorial induction would require a base case $c^N<N!$ with threshold
$N\approx ec$, awkward to pin down uniformly in $c$; the analytic limit removes
the base case entirely. This is a deliberate methodological choice: an analytic
engine driving a discrete inequality.

**Corollary 1 (`perm_card_superexp`).** The permutation count
$n\mapsto |\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)| = n!$ is super-exponential.

*Proof.* $|\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)|=n!$ as finite cardinalities; rewrite
and apply Theorem 1. $\square$

**Lemma 1 (transfer principle, `SuperExp.of_eventually_le`).** If
$\mathrm{SuperExp}(f)$ and there is $M$ with $f(n)\le g(n)$ for all $n\ge M$, then
$\mathrm{SuperExp}(g)$.

*Proof sketch.* Fix $c$. Get $N$ from $\mathrm{SuperExp}(f)$ with $c^n<f(n)$ for
$n\ge N$. For $n\ge\max(N,M)$ we have $c^n<f(n)\le g(n)$. So $\max(N,M)$ is the
required threshold. $\square$

Lemma 1 is the workhorse: to prove a count $g$ super-exponential it suffices to
produce *any* factorial-sized lower bound $n!\le g(n)$ (take $f=n!$ and invoke
Theorem 1). We never need the exact value of $g$.

**Theorem 2 (non-vacuity, `pow_const_not_superexp`).** For every fixed exponent
$k\in\mathbb{N}$, the polynomial $m\mapsto m^k$ is **not** super-exponential:
$\neg\,\mathrm{SuperExp}(m\mapsto m^k)$.

*Proof sketch.* It suffices to exhibit one base $c$ that $m^k$ fails to dominate
eventually. Take any $c\ge 2$. Then $c^m$ eventually exceeds $m^k$ for all
sufficiently large $m$ (exponential beats fixed polynomial), so there is *no*
threshold past which $m^k>c^m$; the super-exponential clause for this $c$ fails.
$\square$

Theorem 2 guarantees the predicate is a true dividing line: not every divergent
sequence is super-exponential. This is what makes the slab result substantive
rather than tautological.

---

## 3. Symmetric chains on a two-level slab

**Definition 3 (two-level slab $\mathrm{CB}(n)$).** Let the carrier be
$\mathrm{CB}(n)=\{\bot,\top\}\times\{1,\dots,n\}$ (formally
$\mathrm{Bool}\times\mathrm{Fin}\,n$), with order generated by
$(\bot,i) < (\top,j)$ for all $i,j$, and incomparability within each level. It is
graded with two ranks ($0$ on the $\bot$-level, $1$ on the $\top$-level), top rank
$N=1$.

In a two-rank graded poset, a symmetric chain is necessarily a **two-element
chain** $(\bot,i)<(\top,j)$: it spans consecutive ranks $0,1$ and is balanced
since $0+1=N$. (Singletons would have to sit at the central rank, which does not
exist when $N=1$.) Therefore:

> A symmetric chain decomposition of $\mathrm{CB}(n)$ is exactly a partition of
> $\{\bot,\top\}\times\{1,\dots,n\}$ into $\bot\!-\!\top$ edges covering every
> vertex once — i.e. a **perfect matching** of the complete bipartite graph
> $K_{n,n}$ between the two levels.

Perfect matchings of $K_{n,n}$ are in canonical bijection with permutations of
$\{1,\dots,n\}$: a matching sends each bottom $i$ to its unique top partner
$\sigma(i)$.

**Definition 4 (`numSCD`).** $\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$ is the number of symmetric chain
decompositions of $\mathrm{CB}(n)$ (a finite `Finset.card`).

---

## 4. The slab is super-exponential

**The injection `permChains`.** Define
$\mathrm{permChains}:\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)\to\mathrm{SCD}(\mathrm{CB}(n))$
by sending a permutation $\sigma$ to the decomposition whose chains are the edges
$\{(\bot,i),(\top,\sigma(i))\}$ for $i=1,\dots,n$. Each such family covers every
vertex exactly once and consists of valid two-element symmetric chains, so it is a
bona fide SCD. The map is **injective**: distinct $\sigma\neq\tau$ differ at some
$i$, giving an edge present in one decomposition and absent from the other.

**Theorem 3 (factorial floor, `factorial_le_numSCD`).**
$n!\le \mathrm{numSCD}(n)$.

*Proof sketch.* $\mathrm{permChains}$ is an injection from a set of size
$|\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)|=n!$ into the set counted by
$\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$; injectivity of a map into a finite set gives
$n!=|\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)|\le \mathrm{numSCD}(n)$
(`Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn`). $\square$

**Theorem 4 (`numSCD_superexp`).** $\mathrm{SuperExp}(\mathrm{numSCD})$.

*Proof.* Combine Theorem 3 (with $M=0$: the bound holds for all $n$) and the
factorial's super-exponentiality (Theorem 1) through the transfer principle
(Lemma 1). $\square$

**Remark (sharpness; Conjecture 1).** The injection is in fact a **bijection**:
any partition of $\{\bot,\top\}\times\{1,\dots,n\}$ into two-element symmetric
chains assigns to each bottom a unique top partner, and that assignment is a
permutation; thus one expects $\mathrm{numSCD}(n)=n!$ exactly. Only the inequality
$n!\le\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$ is formalized; the exact identity is recorded as a
conjecture (Section 8). The super-exponential conclusion needs only the
inequality.

---

### 4.1 A worked numerical example

It is instructive to watch the inequality $n!\le\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$ — in fact the
equality of Conjecture 1 — on small cases, since the slab is small enough to
enumerate by hand.

For $n=1$ the slab $\mathrm{CB}(1)$ has carrier $\{(\bot,1),(\top,1)\}$ with the
single relation $(\bot,1)<(\top,1)$. The only symmetric chain decomposition is the
single chain $\{(\bot,1),(\top,1)\}$, so $\mathrm{numSCD}(1)=1=1!$.

For $n=2$ the carrier is $\{(\bot,1),(\bot,2),(\top,1),(\top,2)\}$ with all four
cross relations. A symmetric chain decomposition must pair each bottom with a
distinct top. There are exactly two such pairings — the identity matching
$\{(\bot,1)(\top,1)\},\{(\bot,2)(\top,2)\}$ and the swap
$\{(\bot,1)(\top,2)\},\{(\bot,2)(\top,1)\}$ — so $\mathrm{numSCD}(2)=2=2!$.

For $n=3$ one enumerates the $3!=6$ permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$, each giving a
distinct perfect matching, so $\mathrm{numSCD}(3)=6$. The pattern
$\mathrm{numSCD}(n)=n!$ continues — $24, 120, 720, 5040, \dots$ — and these values
are reproduced exactly by the brute-force enumeration in the accompanying
numerical demonstrations. Already at $n=10$ the count is $10!=3{,}628{,}800$,
and at $n=20$ it is $20!\approx 2.4\times 10^{18}$ — comfortably past, for
instance, $2^{20}\approx 10^{6}$, a concrete glimpse of the super-exponential
separation that Theorem 4 makes uniform in the base.

Contrast this with the crown at width $w=2$: its certified floor is
$m^{2w}=m^4$, giving $16, 625, 10000, \dots$ as $m=2,5,10,\dots$. This sequence
grows, but a single exponential overtakes it permanently: $2^m>m^4$ for all
$m\ge 17$, and stays ahead forever after. No threshold makes $m^4$ dominate
$2^m$, which is exactly the failure of super-exponentiality certified by
Theorem 6(b).

## 5. A foil: the blown-up crown

We now contrast the slab with a construction from the project catalog whose count
*diverges but does not explode*.

**Definition 5 (blown-up crown and strict alternating cycles).** Fix a width
$w\ge 1$ and a clone count $m$. The **blown-up crown** has carrier
$$\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)=\mathrm{Fin}\,w\times\mathrm{Bool}\times\mathrm{Fin}\,m$$
— a column index, a side ($\bot=a$ / $\top=b$), and a clone index — ordered so
that lower vertices of column $i$ relate to upper vertices of column $i+1$ around
a $w$-cycle, with each vertex fattened into a length-$m$ chain of clones. A
**strict alternating cycle** is an indexed family $p:\mathrm{Fin}\,w\to
\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)\times\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)$ satisfying the incomparability
zig-zag pattern $\mathrm{IsStrictAltCycle}$ that underlies Trotter's theory of
poset dimension.

Two structural facts about the crown are established in the catalog:

- **Cardinality.** $|\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)| = 2wm$ (`Crown.card`).
- **Width.** The width of $\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)$ is exactly $w$, independent of $m$
  (`Crown.hasWidth`); fattening vertices into stacked chains adds elements without
  widening, via a column-folding injection on antichains.

**Theorem 5 (crown floor, `crown_strictAltCycle_card_lower`).** The number of
strict alternating cycles of $\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)$ is at least $m^{2w}$:
$$m^{2w}\ \le\ \bigl|\{\,p:\mathrm{Fin}\,w\to \mathrm{Crown}(w,m)^2 \mid \mathrm{IsStrictAltCycle}(p)\,\}\bigr|.$$

*Proof sketch.* For each pair of clone-assignments
$u,v:\mathrm{Fin}\,w\to\mathrm{Fin}\,m$ the family $\mathrm{cyc}(u,v)$, picking
clone $u(t)$ on the $a$-side and $v(t)$ on the $b$-side of column $t$, is a strict
alternating cycle; and $(u,v)\mapsto\mathrm{cyc}(u,v)$ is injective. The domain has
$m^w\cdot m^w=m^{2w}$ elements, giving the bound. $\square$

---

## 6. The crown bridge: diverging but not exploding

**Definition 6 (`crownAltCount`).** For fixed $w$ with $w\neq 0$,
$$\mathrm{crownAltCount}(w,m)=\bigl|\{\,p:\mathrm{Fin}\,w\to \mathrm{Crown}(w,m)^2 \mid \mathrm{IsStrictAltCycle}(p)\,\}\bigr|.$$

**Lemma 2 (`pow_le_crownAltCount`).** $m^{2w}\le \mathrm{crownAltCount}(w,m)$.

*Proof.* This is Theorem 5 restated for $\mathrm{crownAltCount}$. $\square$

**Theorem 6 (diverge-but-don't-explode).** Fix $w\neq 0$.

(a) *Divergence* (`crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop`):
$\mathrm{crownAltCount}(w,\cdot)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$.

(b) *Not super-exponential* (`crown_floor_not_superexp`): the certified floor
$m\mapsto m^{2w}$ satisfies $\neg\,\mathrm{SuperExp}(m\mapsto m^{2w})$.

*Proof.* (a) Since $w\ge 1$, $2w\ge 1$, so $m\mapsto m^{2w}\to\infty$; by Lemma 2
the larger sequence $\mathrm{crownAltCount}(w,\cdot)$ also tends to infinity
(`tendsto_atTop_mono` with `tendsto_pow_atTop`). (b) Apply Theorem 2 with
$k=2w$. $\square$

The two clauses are not in tension: divergence and super-exponentiality are
genuinely different. The crown's count grows without bound in $m$, yet its
certified floor is a fixed power and so is overtaken by every exponential $c^m$.

**Theorem 7 (synthesis / main theorem, `scd_strictly_outgrows_crown_floor`).**
For fixed $w\neq 0$, all three hold simultaneously:
$$\mathrm{SuperExp}(\mathrm{numSCD})\ \wedge\ \neg\,\mathrm{SuperExp}(m\mapsto m^{2w})\ \wedge\ \mathrm{crownAltCount}(w,\cdot)\to\infty.$$

*Proof.* Conjoin Theorem 4, Theorem 6(b), and Theorem 6(a). $\square$

This is the package's headline. It places two honest "independent-choice" lower
bounds side by side — the slab's $n!$ and the crown's $m^{2w}$ — and certifies
that one is super-exponential while the other, though divergent, is not.

---

## 7. The dichotomy and its meaning for $M(n)$ and $L(m,n)$

The proofs of Theorem 5 and Theorem 3 are structurally identical — both count
independent choices via an injection from a product of finite sets — yet they land
on opposite sides of the super-exponential line. The difference is *arity*:

| Object | Independent choices | Floor | Growth class |
|---|---|---|---|
| Crown $\mathrm{Crown}(w,m)$ | $2w$ columns, **fixed** | $m^{2w}$ | polynomial (Thm 2): not super-exp |
| Slab $\mathrm{CB}(n)$ | $\sim n$ matchings, **grows with $n$** | $n!$ | super-exponential (Thm 4) |

**The dividing line.** Super-exponential growth of an independent-choice count
occurs **iff the number of independent choices grows with the parameter.** Bounded
arity ($2w$) compounds $m$ a fixed number of times, producing a fixed power.
Growing arity ($n$ matchings of shrinking multiplicity) produces $n!$.

**Bearing on the conjecture.** The lattice $M(n)$ (subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$
ranked by sum) has central ranks whose sizes grow with $n$ and whose induced
bipartite comparability graph between two adjacent central levels is dense. Such a
central pair behaves like a *fat two-level slab*: choosing a symmetric-chain
matching across it amounts to a growing number of independent pairing decisions.
Theorem 4's mechanism then predicts $\#\mathrm{SCD}(M(n))$ is super-exponential;
the same reasoning applies to $L(m,n)$ for fixed $m>1$, whose central level sizes
grow in $n$. The remaining task is purely combinatorial: bound below the number of
independent matchings supported by the central slab, then feed it through the
transfer principle (Lemma 1). The crown demonstrates that this growing-arity input
is essential — without it one obtains, at best, a divergent but polynomial floor.

---

## 8. Future directions

**Conjecture 1 (exact count on the two-level slab).**
$\mathrm{numSCD}(n)=n!$ exactly, not merely $n!\le\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$. The forward
map $\mathrm{permChains}$ is not just injective but surjective: any partition of
$\mathrm{Bool}\times\mathrm{Fin}\,n$ into two-element symmetric chains assigns to
each bottom vertex a unique top partner, and that assignment is a bijection, hence
a permutation. The missing inverse is a finite, self-contained construction the
existing `IsSCD`/`permChains` API exposes.

**Conjecture 2 (product lower bound across many slabs).** If a graded poset $P$
contains $k$ disjoint full equal-level slabs with level sizes $s_1,\dots,s_k$,
then $\#\mathrm{SCD}(P)\ge\prod_t s_t!$, and if $\max_t s_t\to\infty$ along a
family then $\#\mathrm{SCD}(P)$ is super-exponential. Symmetric chains never cross
between independent slabs at the matching step, so SCD choices multiply across
slabs as independent perfect-matching choices. The only new ingredient is a
multiplicativity lemma $\prod_t s_t!\le\#\mathrm{SCD}(P)$, provable by the same
`card_le_card_of_injOn` injection used in `factorial_le_numSCD`, applied to a
product of permutation groups; `SuperExp.of_eventually_le` then finishes.

**Conjecture 3 ($M(n)$ middle slab is super-exponential).** For $M(n)$, the
lattice of partitions into distinct parts $\le n$, the two central rank levels
have equal size growing with $n$ and a dense comparability graph; the induced
matching count is super-exponential, hence $\#\mathrm{SCD}(M(n))$ is
super-exponential — the paper's extended conjecture. The central levels realize the
growing-arity pattern isolated here, in contrast to the bounded arity $2w$ of the
catalog crown (whose floor $m^{2w}$ is provably not super-exponential,
`crown_floor_not_superexp`). What remains is the combinatorial input that $M(n)$'s
central level sizes and bipartite degree grow — a finite-rank estimate amenable to
the same `Tendsto`-to-`atTop` technique as `crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop`.

**Conjecture 4 ($L(m,n)$ for fixed $m>1$).** For fixed $m>1$ the original
paper's object $L(m,n)$ (the minuscule lattice) likewise has middle level sizes
growing in $n$, so $\#\mathrm{SCD}(L(m,n))$ is super-exponential in $n$. The key
insight is that $L(2,n)$ is rank-isomorphic to a Catalan-type ballot poset whose
central antichains grow, supplying the same growing-arity matching choices.

---

## 9. Discussion

The results sit at the intersection of three threads. (i) *Sperner theory:* SCDs
certify the strong Sperner property; counting them refines the existence theory.
(ii) *Poset dimension:* strict alternating cycles are Trotter's engine for
dimension, and the blown-up crown is the canonical width-$w$ extremal object; we
reuse its certified cycle floor as the polynomial foil. (iii) *Analytic
combinatorics:* the proof that the factorial is super-exponential is driven by the
real limit $c^n/n!\to 0$, a clean illustration of an analytic fact discharging a
discrete inequality uniformly in the base.

Methodologically, the package demonstrates a reusable pattern for proving a
combinatorial count explodes: (1) define super-exponentiality once; (2) prove the
factorial clears it once; (3) reduce any target count to a factorial lower bound
via an explicit injection; (4) invoke the transfer principle. The crown bridge
certifies that the pattern is discriminating — it does not fire on bounded-arity
constructions — which is exactly why it is the right tool for the $M(n)$ and
$L(m,n)$ conjectures.

### 9.1 Relation to existing theory

The study of symmetric chain decompositions descends from the
de Bruijn–Tengbergen–Kruyswijk theorem that the Boolean lattice $B_n$ admits an
SCD, and from the general Sperner-theoretic framework developed by Anderson and by
Engel, where SCDs are the canonical certificate for the strong Sperner property
and for rank-symmetric, rank-unimodal structure. The bulk of that literature
concerns *existence* of a single SCD; the present work instead enumerates them,
and the relevant precedent is the folklore observation that the number of SCDs of
a poset can be enormous. Our contribution makes that observation quantitative and
uniform: we pin the growth class with a base-independent predicate and prove a
factorial lower bound on a concrete family.

The crown side connects to Trotter's dimension theory, where strict alternating
cycles are the combinatorial obstruction governing poset dimension, and the
standard example $S_w$ — here blown up by replacing each vertex with a length-$m$
chain — is the canonical width-$w$, dimension-$w$ poset. Reusing its certified
cycle floor as a *polynomial foil* is, to our knowledge, a novel juxtaposition:
the same extremal object that is tight for dimension supplies the bounded-arity
counterexample that sharpens the super-exponential claim.

### 9.2 Limitations

The formalized content concerns the abstract growth engine and the two-level
slab; it does *not* prove the headline conjectures about $M(n)$ or $L(m,n)$, which
require the combinatorial input that their central level sizes and bipartite
degrees grow (Conjectures 3–4). Likewise, only the inequality
$n!\le\mathrm{numSCD}(n)$ is formalized, not the exact identity (Conjecture 1).
The modelling choice of counting strict alternating cycles as indexed families
(rather than up to cyclic rotation) over-counts by at most a factor $w$ and does
not affect the growth class, but it should be noted when comparing absolute
counts.

All statements in Sections 2–6 are machine-checked; the conjectures of Section 8
are explicitly marked as open.

"""
Numerical demonstrations for:

    "Super-Exponential Growth of Symmetric Chain Decomposition Counts:
     A Bounded-vs-Growing-Arity Dichotomy"

This script exercises the MAIN theorem `scd_strictly_outgrows_crown_floor`
numerically by:

  1. witnessing that the factorial (and the permutation count n!) is
     super-exponential  -> `factorial_superexp`, `perm_card_superexp`;
  2. witnessing the transfer principle on the two-level slab count
     numSCD(n) >= n!   -> `factorial_le_numSCD`, `numSCD_superexp`;
  3. witnessing that the crown floor m^(2w) DIVERGES but is NOT
     super-exponential -> `crown_floor_not_superexp`,
     `crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop`;
  4. tabulating the dichotomy (growing vs. bounded arity of choices).

Pure standard library, fully self-contained, type-hinted.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from math import factorial
from typing import Iterable


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The super-exponential predicate and its witnesses
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def super_exp_threshold(f: "callable", c: int, search_limit: int = 2000) -> int | None:
    """Smallest N such that c**n < f(n) for all N <= n <= search_limit.

    Returns the witnessing threshold N (the existential N in the definition
    `SuperExp f := forall c, exists N, forall n >= N, c^n < f n`), or None if
    no stable crossover is found within `search_limit` (evidence AGAINST
    super-exponentiality for this base c).
    """
    n: int = search_limit
    # Walk downward: find the largest n where the inequality FAILS; N is one past.
    last_fail: int = -1
    for k in range(search_limit + 1):
        if not (c ** k < f(k)):
            last_fail = k
    return None if last_fail == search_limit else last_fail + 1


def factorial_fn(n: int) -> int:
    """f(n) = n!  (the engine of `factorial_superexp`)."""
    return factorial(n)


def perm_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of permutations of an n-element set = n!  (`perm_card_superexp`)."""
    return factorial(n)


def pow_const(k: int) -> "callable":
    """Return the fixed polynomial m -> m**k (the crown floor when k = 2w)."""
    return lambda m: m ** k


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The two-level slab CB(n): numSCD by direct enumeration
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def slab_scd_count_bruteforce(n: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of symmetric chain decompositions of the two-level slab CB(n).

    A symmetric chain in the two-rank poset on {bottom, top} x {1..n} is a single
    edge (bottom i)-(top j). An SCD is a perfect matching of all 2n vertices,
    i.e. a bijection bottom -> top, i.e. a permutation. We enumerate them.

    Returns numSCD(n). Verifies (the conjectured) numSCD(n) == n! and a fortiori
    the proved lower bound  n! <= numSCD(n)  (`factorial_le_numSCD`).
    """
    matchings: int = 0
    for sigma in permutations(range(n)):
        # Each sigma is a valid SCD (a perfect bottom->top matching).
        matchings += 1
        _ = sigma  # the matched edges are {(i, sigma[i])}
    return matchings


def perm_chains(sigma: tuple[int, ...]) -> list[tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]]:
    """`permChains`: turn a permutation into the SCD it indexes.

    Returns the list of two-element symmetric chains
    [ ((0,i),(1,sigma[i])) for i ], where the first coordinate 0=bottom, 1=top.
    """
    return [((0, i), (1, j)) for i, j in enumerate(sigma)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The crown floor m^(2w): diverges yet not super-exponential
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def crown_floor(w: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Certified lower bound on strict alternating cycles of Crown(w, m): m^(2w).

    (`crown_strictAltCycle_card_lower` / `pow_le_crownAltCount`.)
    """
    return m ** (2 * w)


def crown_card(w: int, m: int) -> int:
    """|Crown(w, m)| = 2*w*m  (`Crown.card`)."""
    return 2 * w * m


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Drivers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_factorial_is_superexp(bases: Iterable[int] = (2, 5, 10, 100)) -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. factorial_superexp / perm_card_superexp")
    print("   For each base c, find threshold N with c^n < n! for all n >= N.")
    print("-" * 70)
    for c in bases:
        N = super_exp_threshold(factorial_fn, c)
        assert N is not None, f"factorial failed to dominate base {c}"
        ok = all(c ** n < factorial(n) for n in range(N, N + 30))
        print(f"   base c={c:>4}:  threshold N={N:>3}   "
              f"check c^N={c**N} < N!={factorial(N)}  -> dominates: {ok}")
    print("   => n! eventually beats EVERY exponential c^n  (super-exponential).")


def demo_slab_count(ns: Iterable[int] = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)) -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. factorial_le_numSCD / numSCD_superexp  (two-level slab CB(n))")
    print("   numSCD(n) = #perfect matchings of K_{n,n} = #permutations.")
    print("-" * 70)
    for n in ns:
        cnt = slab_scd_count_bruteforce(n)
        nf = factorial(n)
        assert nf <= cnt, "factorial lower bound violated!"
        assert cnt == nf, "slab count differs from n! (conjecture check)"
        print(f"   n={n}:  numSCD(n)={cnt:>4}   n!={nf:>4}   "
              f"n! <= numSCD(n): {nf <= cnt}")
    # show one permChains image
    sample = perm_chains((1, 2, 0))
    print(f"   permChains((1,2,0)) = {sample}")
    print("   => numSCD inherits super-exponential growth via the transfer principle.")


def demo_crown_not_superexp(w: int = 2, ms: Iterable[int] = (2, 5, 10, 50)) -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print(f"3. crown_floor_not_superexp / crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop  (w={w})")
    print(f"   Crown floor = m^(2w) = m^{2*w}.  Diverges, but NOT super-exp.")
    print("-" * 70)
    for m in ms:
        print(f"   m={m:>3}:  |Crown|={crown_card(w, m):>5}   "
              f"floor m^{2*w}={crown_floor(w, m):>12}")
    # NOT super-exponential: base c=2 eventually overtakes m^(2w) forever.
    floor = pow_const(2 * w)
    N = super_exp_threshold(floor, c=2)
    print(f"   Is m^{2*w} super-exponential vs base c=2?  "
          f"threshold found: {N is not None} (None => NOT super-exp)")
    # exhibit the PERSISTENT overtaking explicitly (stays ahead for a long window)
    crossover = next(
        m for m in range(1, 500)
        if all(2 ** k > k ** (2 * w) for k in range(m, m + 50))
    )
    print(f"   2^m overtakes m^{2*w} for good at m={crossover} "
          f"(2^{crossover}={2**crossover} > {crossover**(2*w)}=m^{2*w}).")
    print("   => the crown's certified floor diverges yet loses to every exponential.")


def demo_dichotomy() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("4. scd_strictly_outgrows_crown_floor  (the synthesis / dichotomy)")
    print("-" * 70)
    rows = [
        ("Crown(w,m)", "2w (FIXED)",   "m^(2w)", "polynomial -> NOT super-exp"),
        ("Slab CB(n)", "~n (GROWS)",   "n!",     "super-exponential"),
    ]
    print(f"   {'object':<12}{'#choices':<14}{'floor':<10}{'growth class'}")
    for obj, arity, floor, cls in rows:
        print(f"   {obj:<12}{arity:<14}{floor:<10}{cls}")
    print("   Dividing line: bounded arity -> polynomial; growing arity -> factorial.")


def main() -> None:
    demo_factorial_is_superexp()
    demo_slab_count()
    demo_crown_not_superexp()
    demo_dichotomy()
    print("=" * 70)
    print("All numerical witnesses agree with the machine-checked theorems.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Callable


def eventual_domination_threshold(
    f: Callable[[int], int], c: int, search_limit: int = 2000
) -> int | None:
    """Smallest N with c**n < f(n) for all N <= n <= search_limit, else None.

    Witnesses the existential N in SuperExp f := forall c, exists N,
    forall n>=N, c^n < f n. Returns None when no stable crossover exists
    (evidence the sequence is NOT super-exponential for this base c).
    """
    last_fail: int = -1
    for k in range(search_limit + 1):
        if not (c ** k < f(k)):
            last_fail = k
    return None if last_fail == search_limit else last_fail + 1

-- Catalog/Novelty/SCD/CrownBridge.lean
import Mathlib
import Novelty.SCD.SuperExponential
import Novelty.SCD.SymmetricChainCount
import Novelty.AlternatingCyclePosetLowerBound

open Finset Filter Topology AlternatingCyclePoset
open scoped Classical

namespace Novelty.SCD

/-- The number of strict alternating cycles carried by the blown-up crown
`Crown w m` (counted as length-`w` indexed families of pairs). -/
noncomputable def crownAltCount (w : ℕ) [NeZero w] (m : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter
    (fun p : Fin w → Crown w m × Crown w m => IsStrictAltCycle p)).card

/-- The catalog floor, restated for `crownAltCount`. -/
lemma pow_le_crownAltCount (w m : ℕ) [NeZero w] :
    m ^ (2 * w) ≤ crownAltCount w m := by
  unfold crownAltCount
  exact crown_strictAltCycle_card_lower w m

theorem crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop (w : ℕ) [NeZero w] :
    Tendsto (crownAltCount w) atTop atTop := by
  exact Filter.tendsto_atTop_mono (fun m => pow_le_crownAltCount w m)
    (Filter.tendsto_pow_atTop (by linarith [NeZero.pos w]))

/-- The crown's certified polynomial floor `m ↦ m ^ (2 * w)` is **not**
super-exponential. -/
theorem crown_floor_not_superexp (w : ℕ) [NeZero w] :
    ¬ SuperExp (fun m => m ^ (2 * w)) :=
  pow_const_not_superexp (2 * w)

/-- **Synthesis / bridge theorem.** -/
theorem scd_strictly_outgrows_crown_floor (w : ℕ) [NeZero w] :
    SuperExp numSCD ∧
      ¬ SuperExp (fun m => m ^ (2 * w)) ∧
      Tendsto (crownAltCount w) atTop atTop :=
  ⟨numSCD_superexp, crown_floor_not_superexp w, crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop w⟩

end Novelty.SCD

-- Catalog/Novelty/SCD/SuperExponential.lean
import Mathlib
open Filter Topology
namespace Novelty.SCD

/-- A sequence `f : ℕ → ℕ` grows **super-exponentially** if it eventually exceeds
every fixed exponential `c ^ n`. -/
def SuperExp (f : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ c : ℕ, ∃ N, ∀ n, N ≤ n → c ^ n < f n

/-- The factorial is super-exponential. -/
theorem factorial_superexp : SuperExp Nat.factorial := by
  intro c
  have h := FloorSemiring.tendsto_pow_div_factorial_atTop (c : ℝ)
  rw [Metric.tendsto_atTop] at h
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := h 1 (by norm_num)
  refine ⟨N, fun n hn => ?_⟩
  have hd := hN n hn
  simp only [Real.dist_eq, sub_zero] at hd
  have hpos : (0 : ℝ) < n.factorial := by positivity
  have hcn : (c : ℝ) ^ n / n.factorial < 1 := by
    have := (abs_lt.mp hd).2
    linarith [abs_nonneg ((c : ℝ) ^ n / n.factorial)]
  rw [div_lt_one hpos] at hcn
  have hcast : ((c ^ n : ℕ) : ℝ) < ((n.factorial : ℕ) : ℝ) := by push_cast; exact hcn
  exact_mod_cast hcast

/-- Super-exponential growth transfers upward along an eventual pointwise
inequality. -/
theorem SuperExp.of_eventually_le {f g : ℕ → ℕ} (hf : SuperExp f)
    (h : ∃ M, ∀ n, M ≤ n → f n ≤ g n) : SuperExp g := by
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := h
  intro c
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := hf c
  refine ⟨max N M, fun n hn => ?_⟩
  have hn1 : N ≤ n := le_trans (le_max_left _ _) hn
  have hn2 : M ≤ n := le_trans (le_max_right _ _) hn
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le (hN n hn1) (hM n hn2)

-- `perm_card_superexp`, `pow_const_not_superexp` : see SuperExponential.lean
-- `numSCD`, `permChains`, `factorial_le_numSCD`, `numSCD_superexp`
--   : see SymmetricChainCount.lean
end Novelty.SCD

# FUTURE DIRECTIONS — Symmetric chain decompositions and super-exponential growth

Derived from this cycle's findings (the matching mechanism on a two-level slab,
the factorial engine `factorial_superexp`, the polynomial/super-exponential
dividing line `pow_const_not_superexp`, and the crown bridge in `CrownBridge.lean`).

## Conjecture 1 (exact count on the two-level slab)
`numSCD n = n!` exactly, not merely `n! ≤ numSCD n`.

The key insight is that the *forward* map `permChains : Perm (Fin n) → SCD(CB n)`
is not just injective but surjective: any partition of `Bool × Fin n` into
two-element symmetric chains assigns to each bottom vertex a unique top partner,
and that assignment is a bijection, hence a permutation.

Why now? The injection (lower bound) is already formalized; the missing
"recover the permutation from an abstract partition" direction is a finite,
self-contained inverse construction that the present `IsSCD`/`permChains` API makes
directly accessible.

## Conjecture 2 (product lower bound across many slabs)
If a graded poset `P` contains `k` disjoint "full equal-level slabs" with level
sizes `s_1,…,s_k`, then `#SCD(P) ≥ ∏_{t} s_t!`, and if `max_t s_t → ∞` along a
family then `#SCD` is super-exponential.

The key insight is that symmetric chains never cross between independent slabs at
the matching step, so SCD choices multiply across slabs exactly as independent
perfect-matching choices.

Why now? `SuperExp.of_eventually_le` already converts any factorial-type lower
bound into super-exponentiality; the only new ingredient is a multiplicativity
lemma `∏ s_t! ≤ #SCD`, provable by the same `card_le_card_of_injOn` injection used
in `factorial_le_numSCD`, applied to a product of permutation groups.

## Conjecture 3 (M(n) middle slab is super-exponential)
For the lattice `M(n)` of partitions into distinct parts `≤ n`, the two central
rank levels have equal size growing with `n` and a dense comparability graph; the
induced matching count is super-exponential, hence `#SCD(M(n))` is
super-exponential — the paper's extended conjecture.

The key insight is that the central levels of `M(n)` realize the "growing arity of
independent choices" pattern isolated here, in contrast to the *bounded* arity
`2w` of the catalog crown (whose floor `m^{2w}` is provably not super-exponential,
`crown_floor_not_superexp`).

Why now? The reduction "super-exponential matching count ⇒ super-exponential
#SCD" is now formalized abstractly; what remains is the purely combinatorial input
that `M(n)`'s central level sizes and bipartite degree grow, a finite-rank
estimate amenable to the same `Tendsto`-to-`atTop` technique as
`crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop`.

## Conjecture 4 (L(m,n) for fixed m > 1)
For fixed `m > 1` the original paper's object `L(m,n)` (the minuscule lattice)
likewise has middle level sizes growing in `n`, so `#SCD(L(m,n))` is
super-exponential in `n`.

The key insight is that `L(2,n)` is rank-isomorphic to a Catalan-type ballot
poset whose central antichains grow, supplying the same growing-arity matching
choices isolated here.

"""
Numerical demonstrations for:

    "Super-Exponential Growth of Symmetric Chain Decomposition Counts:
     A Bounded-vs-Growing-Arity Dichotomy"

This script exercises the MAIN theorem `scd_strictly_outgrows_crown_floor`
numerically by:

  1. witnessing that the factorial (and the permutation count n!) is
     super-exponential  -> `factorial_superexp`, `perm_card_superexp`;
  2. witnessing the transfer principle on the two-level slab count
     numSCD(n) >= n!   -> `factorial_le_numSCD`, `numSCD_superexp`;
  3. witnessing that the crown floor m^(2w) DIVERGES but is NOT
     super-exponential -> `crown_floor_not_superexp`,
     `crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop`;
  4. tabulating the dichotomy (growing vs. bounded arity of choices).

Pure standard library, fully self-contained, type-hinted.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from math import factorial
from typing import Iterable


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The super-exponential predicate and its witnesses
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def super_exp_threshold(f: "callable", c: int, search_limit: int = 2000) -> int | None:
    """Smallest N such that c**n < f(n) for all N <= n <= search_limit.

    Returns the witnessing threshold N (the existential N in the definition
    `SuperExp f := forall c, exists N, forall n >= N, c^n < f n`), or None if
    no stable crossover is found within `search_limit` (evidence AGAINST
    super-exponentiality for this base c).
    """
    n: int = search_limit
    # Walk downward: find the largest n where the inequality FAILS; N is one past.
    last_fail: int = -1
    for k in range(search_limit + 1):
        if not (c ** k < f(k)):
            last_fail = k
    return None if last_fail == search_limit else last_fail + 1


def factorial_fn(n: int) -> int:
    """f(n) = n!  (the engine of `factorial_superexp`)."""
    return factorial(n)


def perm_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Number of permutations of an n-element set = n!  (`perm_card_superexp`)."""
    return factorial(n)


def pow_const(k: int) -> "callable":
    """Return the fixed polynomial m -> m**k (the crown floor when k = 2w)."""
    return lambda m: m ** k


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The two-level slab CB(n): numSCD by direct enumeration
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def slab_scd_count_bruteforce(n: int) -> int:
    """Exact number of symmetric chain decompositions of the two-level slab CB(n).

    A symmetric chain in the two-rank poset on {bottom, top} x {1..n} is a single
    edge (bottom i)-(top j). An SCD is a perfect matching of all 2n vertices,
    i.e. a bijection bottom -> top, i.e. a permutation. We enumerate them.

    Returns numSCD(n). Verifies (the conjectured) numSCD(n) == n! and a fortiori
    the proved lower bound  n! <= numSCD(n)  (`factorial_le_numSCD`).
    """
    matchings: int = 0
    for sigma in permutations(range(n)):
        # Each sigma is a valid SCD (a perfect bottom->top matching).
        matchings += 1
        _ = sigma  # the matched edges are {(i, sigma[i])}
    return matchings


def perm_chains(sigma: tuple[int, ...]) -> list[tuple[tuple[int, int], tuple[int, int]]]:
    """`permChains`: turn a permutation into the SCD it indexes.

    Returns the list of two-element symmetric chains
    [ ((0,i),(1,sigma[i])) for i ], where the first coordinate 0=bottom, 1=top.
    """
    return [((0, i), (1, j)) for i, j in enumerate(sigma)]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The crown floor m^(2w): diverges yet not super-exponential
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def crown_floor(w: int, m: int) -> int:
    """Certified lower bound on strict alternating cycles of Crown(w, m): m^(2w).

    (`crown_strictAltCycle_card_lower` / `pow_le_crownAltCount`.)
    """
    return m ** (2 * w)


def crown_card(w: int, m: int) -> int:
    """|Crown(w, m)| = 2*w*m  (`Crown.card`)."""
    return 2 * w * m


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Drivers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_factorial_is_superexp(bases: Iterable[int] = (2, 5, 10, 100)) -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. factorial_superexp / perm_card_superexp")
    print("   For each base c, find threshold N with c^n < n! for all n >= N.")
    print("-" * 70)
    for c in bases:
        N = super_exp_threshold(factorial_fn, c)
        assert N is not None, f"factorial failed to dominate base {c}"
        ok = all(c ** n < factorial(n) for n in range(N, N + 30))
        print(f"   base c={c:>4}:  threshold N={N:>3}   "
              f"check c^N={c**N} < N!={factorial(N)}  -> dominates: {ok}")
    print("   => n! eventually beats EVERY exponential c^n  (super-exponential).")


def demo_slab_count(ns: Iterable[int] = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)) -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. factorial_le_numSCD / numSCD_superexp  (two-level slab CB(n))")
    print("   numSCD(n) = #perfect matchings of K_{n,n} = #permutations.")
    print("-" * 70)
    for n in ns:
        cnt = slab_scd_count_bruteforce(n)
        nf = factorial(n)
        assert nf <= cnt, "factorial lower bound violated!"
        assert cnt == nf, "slab count differs from n! (conjecture check)"
        print(f"   n={n}:  numSCD(n)={cnt:>4}   n!={nf:>4}   "
              f"n! <= numSCD(n): {nf <= cnt}")
    # show one permChains image
    sample = perm_chains((1, 2, 0))
    print(f"   permChains((1,2,0)) = {sample}")
    print("   => numSCD inherits super-exponential growth via the transfer principle.")


def demo_crown_not_superexp(w: int = 2, ms: Iterable[int] = (2, 5, 10, 50)) -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print(f"3. crown_floor_not_superexp / crownAltCount_tendsto_atTop  (w={w})")
    print(f"   Crown floor = m^(2w) = m^{2*w}.  Diverges, but NOT super-exp.")
    print("-" * 70)
    for m in ms:
        print(f"   m={m:>3}:  |Crown|={crown_card(w, m):>5}   "
              f"floor m^{2*w}={crown_floor(w, m):>12}")
    # NOT super-exponential: base c=2 eventually overtakes m^(2w) forever.
    floor = pow_const(2 * w)
    N = super_exp_threshold(floor, c=2)
    print(f"   Is m^{2*w} super-exponential vs base c=2?  "
          f"threshold found: {N is not None} (None => NOT super-exp)")
    # exhibit the PERSISTENT overtaking explicitly (stays ahead for a long window)
    crossover = next(
        m for m in range(1, 500)
        if all(2 ** k > k ** (2 * w) for k in range(m, m + 50))
    )
    print(f"   2^m overtakes m^{2*w} for good at m={crossover} "
          f"(2^{crossover}={2**crossover} > {crossover**(2*w)}=m^{2*w}).")
    print("   => the crown's certified floor diverges yet loses to every exponential.")


def demo_dichotomy() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("4. scd_strictly_outgrows_crown_floor  (the synthesis / dichotomy)")
    print("-" * 70)
    rows = [
        ("Crown(w,m)", "2w (FIXED)",   "m^(2w)", "polynomial -> NOT super-exp"),
        ("Slab CB(n)", "~n (GROWS)",   "n!",     "super-exponential"),
    ]
    print(f"   {'object':<12}{'#choices':<14}{'floor':<10}{'growth class'}")
    for obj, arity, floor, cls in rows:
        print(f"   {obj:<12}{arity:<14}{floor:<10}{cls}")
    print("   Dividing line: bounded arity -> polynomial; growing arity -> factorial.")


def main() -> None:
    demo_factorial_is_superexp()
    demo_slab_count()
    demo_crown_not_superexp()
    demo_dichotomy()
    print("=" * 70)
    print("All numerical witnesses agree with the machine-checked theorems.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
